title: Envy and kindness
hookLine: envy sours another's good; kindness enjoys it

cards: The army is coming home. A young shepherd named David has just killed the giant, and King Saul comes home with him.
Women come out dancing with tambourines, singing the kind of line a crowd chants: "Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands." The text gives no sign anyone meant harm by it.
But Saul "was very wroth, and the saying displeased him." Then one short sentence: "Saul eyed David from that day and forward." Nothing bad had happened to Saul.
He'd won. Someone else had simply won more.

teach.b: Envy is a strange sin, because it doesn't even get you anything. Greed wants the thing; envy can't stand that someone else has it.
Thomas Aquinas, the medieval teacher, described it as sorrow over another person's good: their good news lands in you as bad news.
The old Christian lists of deadly sins name envy among them, and Proverbs puts it in the body: "envy the rottenness of the bones." It eats from the inside, and the other person often never knows.
Now look who else stands in that story: Saul's son, Jonathan. If anyone had reason to envy David, it was him. He was the king's son, next in line, and David was the rival for his own future.
Yet "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul."

Jonathan gives David his own robe, and his sword, and his bow. Later, when Saul is hunting David, Jonathan finds him in the wilderness and says, "thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee."
Father and son, the same news, two opposite hearts. Saul saw a threat. Jonathan was glad.
That gladness is what Christians mean by kindness here: not just being nice, but being able to enjoy someone else's good.

teach.h: REJOICE WITH THEM THAT DO REJOICE.
teach.b: Paul puts it in one line to the church in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." For some, the weeping is the easier half.
Celebrating a friend's promotion, the one you wanted, takes something else. That's the cure the tradition offers: not pretending to want less, but practicing being glad.

how: Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs envy with a virtue that answers it, often named kindness or charity, and some preachers point to Jonathan's friendship with David and Paul's call to rejoice with those who rejoice.

o: a bad mood, and being polite to people anyway
a sting at another's good, and gladness at it
wanting things, and sharing yours with others

games.q: the same news, two hearts — tap the pairs.
p: loved him as his own soul
envy the rottenness of the bones

s: envy is just another word for wanting what someone has
wanting the thing is greed. Aquinas described envy as sorrow at another's good: it can't stand that they have it.
Jonathan, the king's son, gave David his robe, sword and bow
the one with the most to lose was the one who was glad.
Saul turned against David because David harmed him
it began with a song. Saul had won too; David had simply won more.

games.q: you're Jonathan, the king's son. everyone is singing about David, the young man who may take the throne that would have been yours. what do you do?
o: keep your distance and watch him.
give him your robe, your sword and your bow.
tell your father he's a danger.
games.why: Jonathan strips off his own robe and gives it to David, with his sword and bow. later he tells him: "thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee."

practice: Choose one person whose good news reached you lately, a new job, a new baby, a win, and version a congratulation in your head that stays about them: no "but", no story about yourself, no comparing.
Try it once more, shorter and warmer. If you pray, you can say Paul's line quietly: rejoice with them that do rejoice.

wordCard.voice: Envy and kindness. Envy is sorrow at another's good; kindness, in Jonathan's way, is gladness at it.

orig.note: Greek: envy, ill will at another's good. The word behind envy in the New Testament's lists of sins.

carryVoice: Your line: their joy is mine. Their good news can be good news for me too. See you tomorrow.
